reports.program: Science, clinical-trial, immigration and infrastructure policy
reports.priceScope: Initial scenario estimate; clinical-trial pathway quantified, other policy benefits not added

what: Institute for Progress develops practical reforms to U.S. science, technology and infrastructure policy.
Its researchers work on scientific funding, high-skilled immigration, biotechnology and the rules governing construction.
For this initial estimate, we quantify a possible clinical-trial acceleration pathway while charging the entire organization’s annual spending.
strengths: An institutional reform can reach many future patients rather than only the people a small service program directly treats.
Its clinical-trial work offers specific proposals, and a new FDA pilot creates an observable implementation opportunity.
Current publications, identifiable staff and IRS filings support that this is an operating research organization.
reservations: No reviewed evidence identifies how much faster an effective treatment would arrive because of an additional donation to IFP.
FDA time savings before a first human trial must not be treated as an equal reduction in final approval time.
The latest extracted financial year is 2023, and large existing grants could reduce the impact of another unrestricted gift.

sections.what:
IFP is a Washington-based nonprofit think tank with several policy teams, not a clinical care provider. Its [organizational description](https://ifp.org/about/) covers innovation, immigration, biotechnology and infrastructure. Its published [clinical-trial agenda](https://ifp.org/the-case-for-clinical-trial-abundance/) examines recruitment, monitoring, trial information, participant compensation and regulator capacity. The useful output is a workable institutional change that allows more informative trials or earlier access to genuinely effective treatment—not a count of policy papers.

We evaluate an ordinary donation to IFP, not a newly invented restricted clinical-trial fund. The model charges the full annual cost benchmark even though only one plausible health pathway is quantified. Immigration, housing, energy and scientific productivity could materially change the result; they are not silently assigned a zero effect.
sections.monitoring:
IFP publishes named research and [current policy analysis](https://ifp.org/why-biotech-companies-go-to-australia-to-test-new-drugs/). This lets a reader inspect proposed changes and identify the agencies involved. It does not establish independent donor attribution or downstream patient outcomes.

The [FDA’s Expedited IND pilot](https://www.fda.gov/industry/fda-actions-accelerate-and-modernize-early-and-late-stage-clinical-development/fda-expedited-investigational-new-drug-ind-pilot-program) independently confirms a live effort to accelerate first-in-human development while protecting participants. We do not credit IFP with creating that pilot. A stronger review would compare the actual reform with IFP’s recommendations, interview implementers, and document timing with and without its contribution. Trial starts, enrollment, informative results and eventual clinical use are distinct milestones.
sections.qualitative:
This is a high-leverage research bet because policy expertise can affect a much larger system than its own budget. Coefficient Giving lists a July 2026 [general-support grant](https://coefficientgiving.org/funds/abundance-and-growth/) to IFP. That verifies funder interest, not GiveBetter’s arithmetic or a guarantee of additional funding room.

The main concern is causal attribution. Regulators, universities, industry, other advocates and existing funders could deliver the same change without a new gift. Relaxing burdens can also damage evidence quality if the wrong protections are removed. An analyst should look for faster reliable information, not simply fewer checks. We would request the next unfunded work package and how it differs from already committed work.
sections.cost:
Our initial health-only estimate is **$3.6M per better life (10 U.S. QALYs)**. This is an explicit scenario, not measured cost-effectiveness. The numerator is the IRS-derived 2023 total expense of $3,079,238; it is a historical organization-wide cost benchmark, not a current budget or donation offer.

For one potentially effective treatment, we assume 100,000 eventual patients, 0.1 QALY gained per patient-year relative to existing care, and six months of earlier availability. We multiply by a 25% chance of useful reform, 10% chance that the affected development produces an effective treatment, 15% IFP attribution, 50% funding additionality and 90% U.S. residence. The result is **8.4375 expected U.S. QALYs**. Every one of these impact inputs is a judgment. FDA’s interest in faster trial starts does not supply them.

The tangible return is research and implementation assistance; the modeled health gain arises only if that work changes policy, the policy changes development, and patients receive effective care sooner. External clinical and implementation costs are not in the donor numerator. They must be added before a societal-cost comparison. Null, adverse, low and favorable cases are shown below; the wide range is not a statistical confidence interval.

**Income and growth.** Immigration and productivity policies may affect earnings. We do not translate national GDP projections into donor-attributable household income. No organization-specific income bridge is populated yet, so the separate [income comparison method](https://ai.rhyslindmark.com/givebetter/methodology/income) contributes no invented uplift.
sections.funding:
The [IRS-derived filing index](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/872449729) reports total expenses of $159,934 in 2021, $1,201,769 in 2022 and $3,079,238 in 2023. These are the latest three extracted calendar-year records located here, not the last three current years. The 2021 startup year makes their $1.5M mean a poor proxy for today’s scale.

**Spending breakdown.** The index reports $405,000 of executive compensation in 2023. We did not obtain an audited allocation between policy teams; no percentage is manufactured. Coefficient Giving’s July 2026 $10.5M general-support commitment is separate from annual expenses, and its duration and restrictions are not established by the fund entry. Do not substitute that grant amount for a one-year operating budget.

The public [giving page](https://givebutter.com/ifp) provides an individual donation route. Before a sizable grant, obtain newer financials, remaining unrestricted runway, team-level costs and an unfunded implementation plan. Current activity is supported by 2026 publications, but marginal capacity remains unverified.

what: 1Day Sooner supports research participants and works to make clinical trials more informative and efficient.
Its U.S. policy program pursues changes to trial evidence, regulatory transparency and participant access.
The organization also works internationally, so this estimate counts only assumed U.S. patient benefit and charges all annual organizational spending.
strengths: Improving clinical research could bring effective treatments to large patient populations sooner.
The organization combines participant-focused work with concrete policy proposals rather than relying only on general awareness.
Its current program activity, financial disclosure and listed Coefficient Giving grant make this a substantive operating research lead.
reservations: Policy activity has not been linked to an independently measured improvement in approval timing or patient health from another gift.
A large part of its mission concerns global research, which cannot all be credited to U.S. residents.
Existing grants, separate advocacy entities, participant harms and downstream development costs complicate a donor-return estimate.

sections.what:
[1Day Sooner’s clinical-trial program](https://www.1daysooner.org/clinical-trial-abundance/) develops proposals to improve evidence generation and access to existing regulatory data. Its broader work includes healthy research participants, challenge studies and partnerships outside the United States. These are different activities; supporting a trial participant is not the same as buying a completed effective treatment.

An ordinary gift supports the organization’s portfolio. The calculation below does not assume a donor can purchase a ring-fenced trial-policy package. It estimates one health pathway while retaining the full annual cost as the numerator. Other benefits are discussed rather than assigned fabricated clinical outcomes.
sections.monitoring:
The [2026 symposium](https://www.1daysooner.org/cta-symposium/) and linked program material document current policy engagement. Its [CTD Commons launch](https://www.1daysooner.org/press-releases/jan-26-ctd-commons-launches-to-unlock-biotechs-lost-archive-and-accelerate-medical-innovation/) describes a concrete effort to make previously inaccessible development information useful. These outputs can be checked, but their existence does not prove that effective treatment arrives earlier.

The next evidence should track which changes become operational, whether researchers use them, trials completed with less delay, and eventual patient use relative to a credible counterfactual. Volunteer recruitment must count eligible people who actually participate, not registrations or expressions of interest. Safety, consent and representation belong in the same monitoring system as speed.
sections.qualitative:
The appealing mechanism is institutional leverage: evidence improvements can affect many development programs. Coefficient Giving’s [fund listing](https://coefficientgiving.org/funds/abundance-and-growth/) records a May 2026 $1.9M clinical-trial policy grant. A funder commitment is a reason to investigate the recipient, not a substitute for a causal estimate.

Participant advocacy is also important because researchers’ incentives need not reflect volunteer welfare. We would be concerned if faster or cheaper studies came at the expense of informed consent or reliable findings. We do not award health credit for a lobbying win alone. IFP and 1Day Sooner work in overlapping ecosystems; their estimated contributions must not be summed as if they produced two independent versions of the same reform.
sections.cost:
Our initial scenario is **$3.2M per better life (10 U.S. QALYs)**. The $2,424,138 numerator is the 2024 total expense reported in the [IRS-derived filing index](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/851103820), not a new grant proposal or current audited budget.

The illustrative pathway is one reform affecting development of a treatment used by 100,000 people, with 0.1 QALY of incremental benefit per patient-year and six months of earlier effective care. We assume a 25% useful-reform probability, 10% clinical-success probability, 20% organization attribution, 50% funding additionality and 60% U.S. patient share. This gives **7.5 expected U.S. QALYs**. The patient volume, health gain, probabilities, contribution, timing and residence split are all judgments—not trial results or Coefficient Giving estimates.

What money buys directly is policy research, implementation assistance and participant-oriented infrastructure. The health effect requires successive links from changed practice to better evidence to effective care received sooner. Failed drug candidates and reforms that do not affect access yield no such benefit. Trial, regulator and treatment costs paid by other actors remain outside this donor-cost calculation.

The low and high scenarios vary those links jointly. They are stress tests, not confidence bounds. We include zero and adverse outcomes instead of presuming reform is always beneficial. No income uplift is added: paying volunteers can be partly a transfer, and no net household-income bridge from another donation was established.
sections.funding:
The [filing index](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/851103820) reports total expenses of $1,554,943 in 2022, $2,832,663 in 2023 and $2,424,138 in 2024. Their three-year mean is approximately $2.3M. The API view lagged the website’s newer year during this review; the 2024 value is attributed to the website extract, not described as a directly inspected original return.

**Spending breakdown.** The 2024 extract lists $452,227 of executive compensation and $565,562 of other salaries and wages, together roughly 42% of expenses. The remaining cost is not divided between programs without full accounts. The [transparency page](https://www.1daysooner.org/finances-transparency/) distinguishes this charity from the separately registered 1Day Action advocacy entity. A gift here is not automatically a gift to that sister organization.

2024 expenses exceeded reported revenue, but this does not establish today’s funding gap: later grants and reserves matter. Request an updated cash forecast, committed grant schedule, allocation by country and program, and the specific work that remains unfunded. The organization’s [donation page](https://www.1daysooner.org/donate/) is live, but no verified scalable new-donor package was located.

reports.priceScope: Initial scenario estimate; energy-related health pathway quantified

what: Foundation for American Innovation develops technology and infrastructure policy proposals for U.S. policymakers.
Its energy work examines permitting, transmission and generation, including the needs of data centers.
We model a possible air-pollution benefit from cleaner generation arriving sooner, while charging its full annual spending.
strengths: Permitting reform can affect infrastructure at a scale much larger than the research budget.
Published proposals identify concrete regulatory barriers and implementation routes.
An identifiable charitable entity, current publications and financial extracts support ongoing operations.
reservations: Natural gas and additional data-center demand mean cleaner air is not an automatic consequence.
No reviewed evidence measures additional clean generation caused by another donation.
The health scenario depends on uncertain attribution, net displacement and local exposure.

sections.what:
FAI is a technology-policy research nonprofit, not an energy developer. Its [organizational description](https://www.thefai.org/about-us) distinguishes it from the affiliated FAI Action advocacy entity. Donors should verify which entity receives their money.

Its [energy-infrastructure memo](https://www.thefai.org/posts/building-baseload-reforming-permitting-for-ai-energy-infrastructure) examines nuclear, geothermal, solar, gas and transmission barriers. A [state supplement](https://www.thefai.org/posts/the-state-permitting-playbook-behind-the-meter-power-supplement) addresses campus-dedicated power. These are proposals, not evidence of additional clean electricity. We evaluate ordinary charitable support, not an invented restricted program.
sections.monitoring:
Named authors and published proposals make the policy mechanism inspectable. They do not establish independently measured adoption, additional generation or donor attribution. A deeper review should match proposals to enacted rules and document whether earlier projects displace dirtier generation or supply new demand.

EPA’s [benefit-evaluation tools](https://www.epa.gov/statelocalenergy/benefit-evaluation-tools-energy-efficiency-and-renewable-energy-policies) offer an appropriate route from generation changes to emissions and health. We have not run AVERT or COBRA; the scenario is not their output.
sections.qualitative:
Specialized policy work can remove bottlenecks affecting large infrastructure investments. Coefficient Giving lists an April 2026 [energy-permitting grant](https://coefficientgiving.org/funds/abundance-and-growth/). That is a sourcing signal, not validation of our estimate.

Faster fossil development and greater power demand can increase exposure, whereas cleaner replacement capacity can reduce it. We do not assume every permitting reform helps health. Other technology-policy effects remain unpriced, rather than being silently treated as zero.
sections.cost:
Our initial health-only scenario is **$49.6M per better life (10 U.S. QALYs)**. The numerator is the IRS-derived 2024 organization expense of $3,719,664, not a current budget or the incremental cost of one reform.

We assume 10 TWh/year of cleaner generation arrives one year earlier, with 50% actually displacing fossil power, 2 premature deaths avoided per displaced TWh and 15 QALYs gained per death avoided. These are illustrative judgments, not an EPA estimate for a named grid. We multiply by 25% useful-reform probability, 10% FAI attribution, 20% funding additionality and 100% U.S. location. The result is **0.75 expected U.S. QALYs**: 10 × 1 × .5 × 2 × 15 × .25 × .1 × .2.

A donation buys policy-research and implementation capacity, not power plants. Health benefits require additional work to change rules, projects to arrive earlier and net harmful emissions to fall. Construction and generation costs are excluded from the donor numerator, so this is not a societal benefit-cost calculation. Induced demand and generation mix can invalidate the central case. Null and harmful scenarios are retained.

**Income and growth.** Energy reliability can affect earnings and productivity, but no organization-specific income bridge is populated. Business revenue is not household welfare; monetized mortality benefits are not income gains.
sections.funding:
The [IRS-derived financial extracts](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/472239840) show expenses of $4,347,192 in 2022, $3,360,231 in 2023 and $3,719,664 in 2024: a mean of approximately **$3.8M**. The web extracts were reviewed; original annual returns were not independently inspected.

**Spending breakdown.** The 2024 extract reports executive compensation of $1,248,309 and other wages of $643,524, together about 51% of expenses. These categories do not identify the energy-team share.

Coefficient Giving’s $2.714M April 2026 commitment is not assumed to be a one-year expense or remaining funding need. The [official giving page](https://www.thefai.org/donate) identifies EIN 47-2239840 and offers financial documents by request. A large grant would require a current budget, existing commitments and a specific additional work plan.
